q: Oxygen is the most abundant element in the Earth’s crust.
e: Oxygen is indeed the most abundant element in the Earth's crust.

q: Oxygen accounts for 31% of the volume of the atmosphere.
e: Oxygen accounts for 21% of the volume of the atmosphere.

q: Oxygen in the combined state exists in water, sand or silica, silicates and rocks.
e: Oxygen is found in various compounds such as water and silicates.

q: Potassium chlorate is safe for the preparation of oxygen in the laboratory.
e: Potassium chlorate is toxic and should not be used for oxygen preparation.

q: Oxygen gas can be prepared from hydrogen peroxide in the laboratory.
e: Oxygen can be generated from hydrogen peroxide using a catalyst.

q: Manganese(IV) oxide is used as a catalyst to slow down the reaction for the preparation of oxygen.
e: Manganese(IV) oxide is used as a catalyst to speed up the reaction.

q: Oxygen is a colorless gas, without taste or smell.
e: Oxygen is indeed a colorless, tasteless, and odorless gas.

q: Oxygen burns easily and does not support combustion.
e: Oxygen does not burn but supports combustion.

q: Metals such as magnesium react with oxygen to form oxides.
e: Metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides.

q: Iron oxidizes rapidly in the presence of air and water, forming hydrated iron(III) oxide.
e: Iron oxidizes slowly to form hydrated iron(II) oxide, known as rust.

q: Phosphorus burns in oxygen to form oxides of phosphorus.
e: Phosphorus reacts with oxygen to produce phosphorus oxides.

q: An oxide is a compound containing oxygen and a metal only.
e: An oxide can contain oxygen and another element, not just metals.

q: Acidic oxides react with basic oxides to give salts only.
e: Acidic oxides react with basic oxides to form salts.

q: Carbon dioxide is a basic oxide.
e: Carbon dioxide is an acidic oxide.

q: Basic oxides are oxides of non-metals.
e: Basic oxides are oxides of metals.

q: Amphoteric oxides can react with both acids and bases.
e: Amphoteric oxides have both acidic and basic properties.

q: Neutral oxides do not react with acids or bases.
e: Neutral oxides are unreactive towards acids and bases.

q: Peroxides react with acids to produce salt and hydrogen gas.
e: Peroxides react with acids to produce salt and hydrogen peroxide.

q: A compound oxide is formed by the combination of two different oxides of different elements.
e: A compound oxide is formed by the combination of two different oxides of the same element.

q: Oxygen is used in steel work and in oxyacetylene gas mixtures for welding.
e: Oxygen plays a crucial role in steel production and welding processes.

q: Liquid oxygen is not used in rockets to support fuel burns.
e: Liquid oxygen is indeed used in rockets to support fuel combustion.

q: Carbon is found in nature as diamond and graphite.
e: Carbon naturally occurs in the forms of diamond and graphite.

q: Fullerene and graphene are naturally occurring forms of carbon.
e: Fullerene and graphene are synthetic allotropes of carbon.

q: All living things have carbon-containing compounds such as carbohydrates and proteins.
e: Living organisms consist of various carbon-based compounds.

q: Diamond is a soft material with a low melting point.
e: Diamond is very hard and has a very high melting point.

q: Graphite is a good conductor of electricity due to the presence of free electrons.
e: Graphite conducts electricity because of its free-moving electrons.

q: Fullerenes are stable and totally unreactive.
e: Fullerenes are stable but not totally unreactive.

q: Graphene is a single layer of graphite and is very strong.
e: Graphene is a monolayer of graphite and is extremely strong.

q: Charcoal is made by heating wood in the presence of air.
e: Charcoal is made by heating wood in the absence of air.

q: Coke is formed from the heating of coal in the absence of air.
e: Coke is produced by heating coal without air.

q: Carbon can be used as a reducing agent in the extraction of metals.
e: Carbon acts as a reducing agent in metal extraction processes.

q: When carbon burns in limited oxygen, carbon dioxide is formed.
e: When carbon burns in limited oxygen, carbon monoxide is formed.

q: Graphite is used in lead pencils because it is soft.
e: Graphite's softness makes it suitable for use in pencils.

q: Diamond is used in jewellery because of its dull appearance.
e: Diamond is used in jewellery because of its brilliant shine.

q: Carbon black is a black powder produced from burning kerosene in limited air.
e: Carbon black is formed when kerosene is burned with limited air.

q: Carbon dioxide is produced when carbon burns in excess air.
e: Burning carbon in excess oxygen produces carbon dioxide.

q: The melting point of graphite is lower than that of diamond.
e: Graphite has a lower melting point compared to diamond.

q: Graphene is a poor conductor of electricity.
e: Graphene is an excellent conductor of electricity.

q: Carbon black is used in making printing ink and black shoe polish.
e: Carbon black is commonly used in inks and polishes.

q: Allotropes of carbon have identical properties.
e: Allotropes of carbon have different physical and chemical properties.

q: Carbon is a major component of macromolecules such as proteins and lipids.
e: Carbon is essential in forming macromolecules in living organisms.

q: Halogens are diatomic molecules and include fluorine, chlorine, bromine, and iodine.
e: Halogens exist as diatomic molecules in their elemental form.

q: Fluorine is a solid at room temperature.
e: Fluorine is a gas at room temperature.

q: Chlorine is a pale green gas with a choking smell.
e: Chlorine has a distinct pale green color and a strong odor.

q: Bromine is a solid at room temperature.
e: Bromine is a liquid at room temperature.

q: Iodine is a purple-black shiny solid that sublimes when heated.
e: Iodine sublimes to form violet vapor when heated.

q: Halogens can be found in nature in their elemental forms.
e: Halogens are not found in nature as elemental forms; they exist as salts.

q: Chlorine is less reactive than fluorine.
e: Fluorine is the most reactive halogen, more so than chlorine.

q: Halogens react with hydrogen to form hydrogen halides.
e: Halogens readily react with hydrogen to form hydrogen halides.

q: Iodine is more reactive than bromine.
e: Bromine is more reactive than iodine.

q: Chlorine can displace bromine from sodium bromide solution.
e: Chlorine is more reactive and can displace bromine from its compounds.

q: Bromine is a stronger oxidizing agent than chlorine.
e: Chlorine is a stronger oxidizing agent than bromine.

q: Halogens react with alkalis to form halides.
e: Halogens react with alkalis to produce halides.

q: The presence of halide ions can be tested using silver nitrate solution.
e: Silver nitrate solution is used to test for halide ions.

q: Chlorine does not have bleaching properties.
e: Chlorine has strong bleaching properties.

q: Bromine reacts with metals to form metal bromides.
e: Bromine reacts with metals to form corresponding bromides.

q: The reactivity of halogens decreases from fluorine to iodine.
e: The reactivity of halogens decreases in the order of F, Cl, Br, I.

q: Halides are positively charged ions formed from halogens.
e: Halides are negatively charged ions formed from halogens.

q: Iodine can displace chlorine from sodium chloride solution.
e: Iodine cannot displace chlorine from sodium chloride solution.

q: Chlorine reacts with water to form hydrochloric acid and hypochlorous acid.
e: Chlorine reacts with water to produce HCl and HOCl.
